idiom_name: unexported identifiers plus the go command's internal/ directory rule; export_test.go for white-box tests
implementation_notes: Go offers exactly two access forms - unexported (package-local) and exported - and the language cannot enforce anything finer; the Go 1.4 release notes say so outright: 'The Go language does not have the power to enforce this distinction.' What replaces the classic structure is placement plus the go command's internal rule: a package whose path contains an internal directory may be imported only by code in the tree rooted at that directory's parent, so an implementation package under internal/ is callable by the helper subtree and invisible to the module's consumers. The hand-built attorney is still justified when one helper only should call one operation: export the single narrow door from an internal package, keep everything else unexported, and accept that the grant is subtree-granular rather than helper-granular.
pitfalls: The internal rule is enforced by the go command while resolving imports, not by the language: other tooling, a vendored copy or a symlinked path steps around it, and nothing in the compilation rejects the import.
Granularity is the subtree: every package under the internal root may import the implementation, and a package added there later silently receives the grant.

Test files in the same package can reach unexported identifiers (the export_test.go alias trick), but aliases exported there are visible to every test file of that package, and they are a test-only door - do not turn them into API.
